name: Ivan Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Ivan. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: No problem. I'm Ivan, I'm 27, and I run the cattle at Oakfield Farm. We've got about 280 suckler cows, meaning cows that rear their own calves, on rented grassland. We make our own hay and silage, and grow a bit of barley for feed. I've got two lads working with me, and the owner, Mr Kovac, mostly leaves the herd to me now.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Let's start simple. Walk me through a normal working day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mornings I check the cows and calves, and in calving season that's every three hours, day and night. Then it's feeding, moving groups between fields, fixing fences and water troughs. In June and July we're making hay and silage whenever the weather allows, which is all hands, with the contractor's baler coming in. I love a field of good calves at weaning, all even and healthy. What wears me out is the price of fertiliser and feed, which can wipe out a good year.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who's at home, and how do you use AI, if at all?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with Mira, my girlfriend, who's an accountant at a firm in town. I use AI now and then, mostly to check a vet question or to look at the weighing data from the scales. I wasn't the first to try it, I waited until our vet started using it. We've got about four months of money saved between us, a bit more on her side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. We call this one AI Plateau.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That wouldn't surprise me at all, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful tool for the paperwork, and that's about it. Cattle still need someone watching them, and you can't feed a cow with a chatbot. I'd say it at the market and I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved, mostly for Mira. Her job is the one people say AI will do. For me, I'd be a bit disappointed there's no better way to spot a sick calf before it's too late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going. Maybe use the weighing data a bit more, the way the vet showed me. Mira and I would keep saving, and I'd still be looking at buying 20 cows of my own to run alongside Mr Kovac's herd in a couple of years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a dry week for hay with the baler booked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Twenty cows of your own. How would that work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mr Kovac has said I can graze some of my own on his land if I pay rent per head. It's how a lot of young farmers start. Twenty cows is maybe a year's savings, so it'd be a stretch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything change for the lads working with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. They'd carry on, and I'd keep training them. One of them, Petr, is going to be better than me with cattle in a few years.

S0.say: I'd say it's a useful tool for paperwork and that's about it. Cattle still need someone watching them, and you can't feed a cow with a chatbot.
S0.think: Privately I'd be relieved, mostly for Mira, whose accountancy job is the one people say AI will do. I'd be a bit disappointed there's no better way to spot a sick calf early.
S0.do: Keeps going and uses the cattle weighing data a little more. Keeps saving with Mira and plans to buy 20 cows of his own to graze on his employer's land within a couple of years.
S0.feel: Calm, like a dry week for hay with the baler booked.
S0.quote: Cattle still need someone watching them, and you can't feed a cow with a chatbot.
S0.fieldNote: Ivan is level-headed and thinks about his partner's job as much as his own. His long-term plan is to build his own herd slowly on his employer's land. He adopts tools once someone he trusts, like the vet, has shown they work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. We call this one Steady Disruption.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. That one's more likely, if you ask me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a change like the one when everyone went from small bales to big ones. Some people grumbled, some got left behind, most adjusted. I'd say let's be sensible and not buy everything the first year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the cattle work would be fine for a good while, but Mira's job would change a lot. Cameras and collars on cows, maybe, but someone still needs to calve a heifer at three in the morning. I'd be more worried about our household money than my own job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait until a couple of farms nearby had collars on their cows that warn you about sickness and calving, then I'd ask Mr Kovac to try them. I'd still buy my first 20 cows, but maybe a year later than planned. And I'd tell Mira to start looking at what parts of her job are safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. More for us as a couple than for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Mira say to that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say she already knows, thank you very much. She's sharper than me about money. She'd probably end up moving into advising farmers on their accounts, because they'd still want to talk to a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame, if it went badly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know that I'd blame anyone in particular. Companies do what saves money, governments are always late. I'd just want the support to be there for people who need it.

S1.say: I'd say it's like when everyone went from small bales to big ones: some grumbled, some got left behind, most adjusted. Be sensible and don't buy everything the first year.
S1.think: Privately I think cattle work would be fine for a good while, but Mira's accountancy job would change a lot. I'd worry more about our household money than my own job.
S1.do: Waits until nearby farms use health and calving collars, then asks his employer to try them. Delays buying his first 20 cows by a year and encourages Mira to work out which parts of her job are safe.
S1.feel: Uneasy, more for the household than for himself.
S1.quote: Someone still needs to calve a heifer at three in the morning.
S1.fieldNote: Ivan compares this to an earlier farm change, big bales, which fits his steady, measured style. His worry shifts to his partner's work rather than his own. He blames no one in particular, which matches his centre outlook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. We call this one AGI by 2028.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's quick. That's before I've even got my own cows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a sensible plan from government, fast, and people shouldn't panic-sell their herds. Food still needs producing. I'd say keep calm and talk to your bank before you do anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think Mira's job goes first and then mine, maybe a year later. If a robot can calve a heifer, Mr Kovac will buy one. I'd be honest with myself that my plan for my own herd is gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd drop the plan to buy cows straight away and keep the money in the bank. I'd ask Mr Kovac what he's thinking and offer to set up whatever machines he buys. Mira and I would cut back, no holiday, and put the wedding we've talked about on hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd still be getting up and doing the work, but it'd be heavy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned a wedding. Is that something you'd planned?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not planned, but talked about, for next summer maybe. In that picture we'd wait. I wouldn't want to spend twelve thousand on a party with both our jobs going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you turn for help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Family first. My parents have a small farm, a few cows and some land. We could live there if we had to. It wouldn't feel good at 28, but it's better than nothing.

S2.say: I'd say we need a sensible plan from government, fast, and people shouldn't panic-sell their herds. Talk to your bank before you do anything.
S2.think: Privately I think Mira's job goes first and mine maybe a year later. If a robot can calve a heifer, Mr Kovac will buy one, and my own herd plan is gone.
S2.do: Drops his plan to buy cows and keeps the money in the bank. Offers to set up whatever machines his employer buys, cuts household spending, postpones a wedding, and keeps his parents' small farm as a fallback home.
S2.feel: Anxious and heavy, but still getting up and working.
S2.quote: I wouldn't want to spend twelve thousand on a party with both our jobs going.
S2.fieldNote: In the fastest picture Ivan's household faces two job losses, and his reaction is to protect cash and delay big life plans. He still offers to help bring in the machines, a practical move rather than a fight. His safety net is his parents' farm rather than the state.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. We call this one AGI by 2031.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is a bit better. Not much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years to work out what farming looks like after this, so let's do it properly. Farmers should talk to each other and not all buy the same kit at the same time. I'd say that at the discussion group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years means I can still buy a few cows, but I'd want to be careful. Maybe the value is in owning the animals and the land, not doing the work. That's a strange thought for someone who loves the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd buy ten cows instead of twenty, to keep more cash. I'd learn the new health collars and the feeding robots once the farm next door had them working. Mira would take a course in something less exposed, maybe farm business advice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'd be planning, but I'd keep checking the news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the value might be in owning, not working. Can you say more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If machines do the work, then whoever owns the cows and the land gets the money. People like me, who only have the skills, lose out. So maybe I'd try to own a bit, even small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is that a risk with only four months saved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. Ten cows is still a big chunk. If it went wrong we'd have a month left, and that's scary. I'd only do it if Mira's job looked steady for a couple of years.

S3.say: I'd say we've got a few years to work out farming after this, so do it properly. Farmers should talk to each other and not all buy the same kit at once.
S3.think: Privately I think the value might end up in owning the animals and land, not doing the work. That's a strange thought for someone who loves the work.
S3.do: Buys ten cows instead of twenty in the first year to keep more cash. Learns the health collars and feeding robots once a neighbour has them working, while Mira retrains towards farm business advice.
S3.feel: Uneasy, planning but checking the news often.
S3.quote: If machines do the work, then whoever owns the cows and the land gets the money.
S3.fieldNote: Five years pushes Ivan towards owning something, however small, because he sees that skills alone may not pay. He'd still take the cautious route: fewer cows, more cash kept back. His plans depend on his partner's job holding, which ties both careers together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. We call this one AGI by 2036.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be 37. I could have a proper herd by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to get ready without panicking. Young farmers should be helped to own land and stock now, while there's time. I'd want the government and the banks to back that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years feels like a fair chance. I'd get my herd going, learn the new kit as it comes, and be in a good spot when it arrives. I think I'd come out of it okay, which I wouldn't say out loud in case it sounds smug.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd buy my 20 cows as planned. Over the next five I'd grow to maybe 60, and bring in the collars and a feeding robot once they're proven nearby. Mira and I would get married, buy a house, and probably start a family around year three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. I'd still want to keep an eye on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does having ten years change anything about family plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It makes it easier. With two years we'd wait for everything. With ten, we'd just get on with life and plan around it, like you plan around a dry summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you change your mind and slow down?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the farms near us started laying people off early, in year four or five. That's when I'd stop buying cows and hold cash. I'd want to see it before I reacted, that's how I am.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough to get ready without panicking. Young farmers should be helped to own land and stock now, with government and banks behind them.
S4.think: Privately, ten years feels like a fair chance to build my herd and learn the new kit. I think I'd come out okay, though I wouldn't say so in case it sounds smug.
S4.do: Buys his first 20 cows in year one and grows to about 60 over five years, adding collars and a feeding robot once proven nearby. Marries Mira, buys a house and plans a family around year three, ready to hold cash if local layoffs start.
S4.quote: With ten, we'd just get on with life and plan around it, like you plan around a dry summer.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years lets Ivan follow his original plan: own a herd, marry, start a family. He's quietly confident but sets a clear signal for slowing down, layoffs on nearby farms. His steady style shows in wanting to see change before reacting.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because both our jobs would go at once and we'd have no time to own anything. What would help is help for young farmers to buy land and stock, so people like me aren't just selling our skills when the machines can do them for free.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about Mira. Everyone talks about farm jobs, but office jobs like hers might go first. Our plans only work if both of us are okay.

headlineQuote: If machines do the work, then whoever owns the cows and the land gets the money.
portrait: Ivan is a 27-year-old cattle manager on a beef and hay farm, living with his girlfriend Mira, an accountant. He's pragmatic, blames no one in particular, and adopts new tools once someone he trusts has proved them. His plan to build a small herd of his own runs through every scenario, shrinking or vanishing as the warning time gets shorter. He comes to see that owning stock and land may matter more than skill, and he worries about Mira's job as much as his own.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because both his and Mira's jobs would go at once and there'd be no time to own anything.
whatWouldHelp: Support for young farmers to buy land and livestock, so they aren't only selling skills that machines can provide for free.
